catalog_quote: So far, the data exhibits a considerable number of minimal sets showing the presence of a three-way tonal contrast, High, Mid and Low, in the language. ... It is also noteworthy that in the disyllabic roots in Champang, the tonal contrasts are mostly found on the most prominent syllable, i.e., the stronger syllable, which in this case is the second syllable. The initial syllable or the prefix /ə-/ is weak in the sense that it is not stressed, and hence, it is either toneless or it replicates the tones carried by its corresponding second syllable. In case of [ətiŋ], the initial syllable is not considered because its pitch height isn’t measurable in PRAAT.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Champang is described as tonal (tentative three-way High/Mid/Low contrast). In disyllabic roots of the shape ə- + root syllable, the second (final, root) syllable is the prominent/stressed syllable and carries the tonal contrast; the initial ə- presyllable/prefix is unstressed and toneless (or copies the following tone). This is an iambic/sesquisyllabic prominence statement restricted to ə-initial disyllables; the paper gives no general rule for stress in other polysyllables or compounds (e.g. /punu/ 'snake', /péwé/ 'peas').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; author flags the whole tone analysis as 'still in progress' and 'tentative' (fn. v, p. 200), tones not marked on obstruent-coda syllables. Note the conflicting first-hand reports on tone: Morey 2014 (p. 666) could not posit tonal categories and van Dam 2018 (sec. 8.1, pp. 203-206) concludes Champang and Chamkok lack phonemic tone, whereas Begum 2023 argues tone exists; all three agree the initial ə-/presyllable is weak (van Dam 2018 p. 94: 'The presyllable is toneless and unstressed'; Morey 2014 pp. 666-667: low level first syllable, step up to a higher falling pitch on the second syllable of Champang disyllabic nouns).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (disyllabic roots elicited in isolation and measured in Praat); statement concerns citation forms of ə-prefixed disyllabic roots, not phrase-level prominence. Variety: Champang (Thamphang) as spoken in Malong/Yopakan area, Assam-Arunachal border, India.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand prosodic statements concern Champang (Thamphang; Glottolog lists 'Champang = Olay = Nahenic [NOCODE_Nahenic]') as spoken by the small migrant community at Malong-I (Tinsukia, Assam) and Yopakan (Changlang, Arunachal Pradesh), India; van Dam 2018 sec. 8.2 adds tone data for Haqchum (speaker from Pangsau, Myanmar). Glottolog's nahe1238 'Nahenic' lumps Champang, Chambok/Chamkok, Lumnu, Haqchum, Longpan, Tokhe and Nahen; van Dam 2018 (p. 206-207) reports that Nahen itself may be closer to Lainong than to Champang-Haqchum, so the Champang statement should be catalogued as Champang (Champhangic) rather than as Nahen proper. The sources disagree on whether Champang is still tonal (Begum 2023: yes, tentative 3 tones; Morey 2014 and van Dam 2018/2026: tone lost).

sources.note: Sec. 6 'Tone in Champang' (pp. 200-205): argues for a three-way High/Mid/Low tonal contrast (tentative). Sec. 6.1 pp. 201-202: in disyllabic roots the tonal contrast sits on 'the most prominent syllable, i.e., the stronger syllable, which in this case is the second syllable'; the initial syllable/prefix /ə-/ 'is weak in the sense that it is not stressed' and is toneless or copies the tone of the second syllable. No general statement of stress placement in other polysyllables/compounds.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2018. The tone system of Tangsa-Nocte and related northern Naga varieties. PhD thesis, La Trobe University. xviii+315 pp. doi:10.26181/21858474.v1
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 5.1.3 p. 94 (all Tangsa-Nocte): 'The presyllable is toneless and unstressed'. Sec. 8.1 pp. 203-206: Champang (consultants in Malong-I, Assam) 'appears to have lost lexical tone entirely.. Champang, along with the Chamkok variety, is lacking any system of phonemic tone'; no statement of where stress falls. Sec. 8.2 pp. 206-215: Haqchum retains a reduced tone system (tones 1 and 3 possibly merged), tone contours neutralised 'in the onset position of a prosodic word'; nothing on stress placement.

sources.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2014. Studying tones in North East India: Tai, Singpho and Tangsa. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 637-671. hdl:10125/24619
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 666-667: Champang nouns are disyllabic; F0 pattern 'remarkably similar' across words: 'a more or less level pitch on the first syllable, in the lower range of the speaker's voice, and then a step up and a higher falling tone in the second syllable' -- so ubiquitous that tone may no longer be functional; no tonal categories could be posited. Describes a fixed word melody with the pitch event on the final syllable but does not use the word stress for Champang.
